title: Nuclear Weapons & Deterrence
hook: How do you stop a war you could never survive? The nuclear age answered with a chilling paradox: build weapons so terrible that no one dares use them.
key_points: Deterrence is preventing an attack by threatening unacceptable retaliation.
Nuclear deterrence rests on the credible threat of devastating response.
'Mutually assured destruction' (MAD): if both sides would be destroyed, neither attacks.
It is stabilizing in theory but fragile — depending on rationality, signaling, and avoiding accidents.
content_html: Nuclear weapons transformed the logic of war because their destructive power is so vast that a full exchange could not be "won" in any meaningful sense. Out of that grim fact emerged the strategy that has shaped great-power security ever since: deterrence. Deterrence is the idea of preventing an attack not by defending against it but by threatening a response so costly that a rational adversary chooses not to attack in the first place. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes it as a strategy built on credible threat rather than active use.
extra_html: Nuclear deterrence took this to its extreme conclusion in the doctrine of "mutually assured destruction," or MAD. If two adversaries each possess enough nuclear weapons to devastate the other even after absorbing a first strike, then neither can hope to gain by attacking — any attack would guarantee its own annihilation in return. The paradox is that safety comes from each side's vulnerability: the very impossibility of surviving a war is what prevents it. During the Cold War this logic is widely credited with helping keep an uneasy peace between nuclear-armed superpowers. But deterrence is more fragile than its tidy logic suggests, and understanding its weaknesses matters as much as its strengths. It assumes decision-makers are rational and well-informed; it depends on each side correctly reading the other's intentions and capabilities (a failure of signaling can be catastrophic); and it is vulnerable to accidents, technical errors, and the spread of weapons to more actors, including ones harder to deter. Deterrence thus offers a sobering case study in how states try to buy security through threat — and why that security can never be taken for granted.

related.title: War & Peace
related.hook: War is politics at its most extreme — organized violence between groups. Understanding why it happens, and how peace is kept, is central to the study of states.

related.title: Diplomacy & War
related.hook: States pursue their interests on a spectrum that runs from the conference table to the battlefield. Diplomacy and war are two ends of the same toolkit.

related.title: Terrorism
related.hook: Terrorism is violence aimed less at its victims than at an audience — using fear as a political weapon to force change a group cannot win by other means.

flashcards.back_html: Preventing an attack by threatening retaliation so costly that the attacker decides it isn't worth it.

choices.text: If both sides would be destroyed in a nuclear exchange, neither has reason to start one
Both sides agree to destroy their weapons
One side can win a nuclear war cheaply

flashcards.explanation_html: MAD holds that when each side can annihilate the other even after being struck first, starting a war becomes suicidal — and so is deterred.

flashcards.prompt: Why is nuclear deterrence considered fragile despite its logic?

choices.text: It depends on rational actors, clear signaling, and avoiding accidents or miscalculation
Because the weapons do not actually exist
Because it has no effect on behavior

flashcards.explanation_html: Deterrence can fail through misperception, irrational actors, technical accidents, or proliferation — so its stability is never guaranteed.
